# ADR-0078: The hard-tools-only engine build for external clusters

> **Status:** accepted | **Date:** 2026-11-19

**References:** [RFC-0001:C-INFERENCE](../rfc/RFC-0001.md#rfc-0001c-inference), [RFC-0001:C-ROUTE](../rfc/RFC-0001.md#rfc-0001c-route), [RFC-0002:C-PLAYBOOK-CAPS](../rfc/RFC-0002.md#rfc-0002c-playbook-caps), [ADR-0065](../adr/ADR-0065.md), [ADR-0021](../adr/ADR-0021.md)

## Context

An engine deployed on a cluster we manage is trusted with model credentials because we control the cluster. An external cluster is not ours: an operator there, or anyone who takes a pod, would hold whatever the deployment carries — and what a dispatch carries today is spend: the controller resolves providers for every pod and hands the engine the inference document with their keys ([ADR-0065](../adr/ADR-0065.md)), and the engine relays agent-visible secrets into sandboxes.

But an external cluster is still useful as a place to run the hard tools: the command-shaped work of a playbook — builds, tests, measures, reports — which needs no model at all. A run with no agent binding already reaches its model the way its manifest and the ambient environment say ([RFC-0001:C-INFERENCE](../rfc/RFC-0001.md#rfc-0001c-inference)), so on an external cluster the engine must instead be one that cannot reach a model, whatever its environment says and whatever a pack asks for. And model keys are not the only reach a dispatch carries: the run's own token, the git sidecar's GitHub credential, per-task tokens for the run's servers. On a cluster we do not manage, the engine must authenticate as nothing.

The engine binary already has one build axis: without `autoresearch` it is the playbook workflow engine. The model surface cuts across that axis — agent tasks and model-decided routes run in playbook runs too — so it needs its own.

## Decision

A cargo feature `agents`, on by default, carries the engine binary's model surface: agent turns, model-decided routes, and the `[agent]` configuration that reads and relays credentials. `autoresearch` implies it. The external-cluster build omits it — `cargo build -p crucible --no-default-features --features hard-tools-only`, where `hard-tools-only` names the build and carries nothing — and is the **hard-tools-only engine**.

The hard-tools-only engine refuses, fail-closed, every plan task that asks a model: an agent turn, a model-decided route ([RFC-0001:C-ROUTE](../rfc/RFC-0001.md#rfc-0001c-route)), and the scored loop's propose turn — exactly the tasks `TaskKind::spends` marks, the ones that draw on the cost ceiling. `crucible plan run` refuses the plan before dispatch with an error naming the task and the kinds that do run; `crucible check` reports each such task as a finding, so a pack this build cannot run does not pass check on it; the task runner refuses again as a backstop, so no caller reaches a model surface. This mirrors [RFC-0002:C-PLAYBOOK-CAPS](../rfc/RFC-0002.md#rfc-0002c-playbook-caps): a capability the substrate does not have truncates the plan before any spend, only here the capability is absent by build rather than by dispatch.

Beyond the model surface, the build authenticates as nothing. It reads no inference document, so the decision capability is not its to grant, and it applies no `[agent]` table: no harness pinning, no skills toolbox, no `[agent].env` or secret relay, no `[mcp]` servers. `--agent-cmd`, `--harness`, and `--model` are refused. It reaches no agent servers: a server the controller grants is refused at run start, naming the grant, and a pack naming `[workflow].servers` is refused before any work — so the git sidecar and buildit never start and no task token is minted. It opens no decision desk and reads no run token: a human-decided route cannot run on it (a required one truncates the plan through the same missing-capability path, an advisory one is skipped with its dependents), it delivers no run evidence, and `--rerun-of` must name a local state directory rather than evidence on the controller. The S3 surface is absent from the build entirely: no `fetch`, no run publishing, no AWS SDK linked, so not even an ambient cloud credential has a reader.

Command, evaluate, and report tasks, and output-decided routes, run as before. The refusal is at plan admission, not in the compiler: the library stays feature-free, so a controller links the same library and validates every pack, whatever build its images run.

## Consequences

- The library, the workflow compiler, and the controller are unchanged; only the binary's behavior differs per build, and the default build is byte-for-byte its former self.
- The agent modules stay compiled in the hard-tools-only binary — the reporter, control, and openshell layers share their event types — but no path reaches them: admission, check, and the runner all refuse first, and no credential the environment carries has a reader. Tests that exercise agent behavior are gated to the `agents` build, and CI clippies and tests the stripped feature set so it cannot quietly break.
- A run on this build is fire-and-forget: it reports nothing home, and its results live only where the pack writes them (its declared outputs and files). A launch dispatched to such a target by today's controller would deliver the inference document, the run's servers, and the pod token, all of which the engine refuses or never reads; the run then proceeds, or refuses loudly when a granted server or a model-asking task meets the admission checks. Dispatch-side policy — resolve no models, deliver no run secrets or servers to such a target — remains the follow-up, now as hygiene and a clean pod rather than as the safety property itself.
- A pack with agent tasks or a required human decision fails on a hard-tools-only engine at plan load, minutes later than an API-side refusal would and with no spend; its author gets the task name and the kinds that run instead.
- Dropping `publish` from the build removes the bin's `required-features` crutch: the binary now compiles with no features at all, and `--no-default-features --features hard-tools-only` is the documented, self-naming form of the stripped build.
- The image build carries the feature set as a build-arg (`ENGINE_FEATURES` on the self-contained runtime Containerfile), so the external-cluster image is one build-arg away from the standard one.

## Alternatives Considered

### A default-on `agents` feature; the external-cluster build omits it, refuses model-asking tasks at admission, check, and the runner, and authenticates as nothing (accepted)

- **Pros:** The default build is untouched, so nothing we run today changes., The refusal is typed and names the task, the build, and what runs instead, at the same place missing capabilities already truncate a plan., No library split: the controller keeps one library that validates every pack., Nothing delivered can activate anything: the engine refuses grants it cannot honor and reads no token at all.

### Refuse at run time, keyed on an environment variable or profile (rejected)

- **Rejected because:** The switch ships inside the full engine, so the external deployment would still be the full engine: whoever controls the pod controls the switch, and the ambient-credential path ([RFC-0001:C-INFERENCE](../rfc/RFC-0001.md#rfc-0001c-inference)) is one flip away.

### Compile the agent modules out of the binary entirely (rejected)

- **Rejected because:** The reporter, control, and openshell layers share the agent event types, so the surgery would reach far past the model surface. The admission and runner refusals already leave no reachable path, which is the guarantee compilation would buy.

### Keep the command-task services (git sidecar, task tokens, buildit) and the pod token, delivery-gated, and strip credentials at dispatch only (rejected)

- **Rejected because:** The engine would still use whatever the environment carries, so an external deployment's safety would rest on delivery discipline alone, with no refusal to catch a miss. A grant silently ignored is a grant still delivered.
